body:
Two commits. The first expands the cycle from 12 days to 16. The second fixes the
reason that was dangerous to do.

## Why the second commit exists

The cycle was addressed positionally in three places that could disagree: a bundled
`DAY_CONFIG`, a bundled `DAY_DESIGN`, and loose `workout-day-definition` documents.
Moving a day silently repointed every exercise and every logged workout at whichever
day took its slot. Applying a change meant clicking an admin button that deleted all
the data and reinserted it from `seed-data.js`, with no record of what ran or whether
it finished.

So a 12→16 renumber wasn't a data change, it was an unversioned rewrite of live
production data with no way to tell afterwards what had happened.

## What changed

**Days have a permanent slug.** The number is only a day's position in one version of
the model. Reordering the cycle changes numbers and nothing else.

**The cycle is data.** A `workout-model` document per generation, exactly one active.
Synergy 12 is retired rather than deleted, so a workout logged under Torso in 2025
still resolves to Torso.

**Logs are faithful records.** Each stores `daySlug`, `dayNumber`, `dayName` and
`modelVersion` as they were on the day it happened. Nothing later edits them.

**Migrations replace the seed step.** Numbered, forward-only, shipped in the same image
as the code that expects them, run at pod startup before any route is mounted. A
failure exits the process and fails the rollout — a half-migrated database serving
traffic is worse than a deploy that stops.

Cosmos has no cross-document transaction, so a migration can die partway and be retried
from the top. Each one is written to survive that, and `npm run migrate:dry-run` proves
it by replaying against the already-migrated result.

Migrations auto-apply only in the cluster (`RUN_MIGRATIONS_ON_BOOT`). Local development
points at the live database, so `npm run dev` reports what's pending instead of applying
it — otherwise starting a dev server on a branch would push a half-written migration to
production.

## Verification

`npm run migrate:dry-run` reads production read-only, runs both migrations in memory,
prints the resulting cycle, and replays them to check they're safe to retry.

It caught a real bug before it shipped: Dumbbell Bench Press legitimately sits on two
days (Pecs Mobility at 20lb, and Push), and the first version of 002 collapsed them into
one entry and then tried to delete the same document twice.

The app was then built against a snapshot generated from the post-migration data and
loaded as an anonymous visitor: 16-segment dial, D11 Pecs (Mobility) as today, 52
exercises across 16 day filters, Cycle tab rendering entirely from the model. History
keeps its own past — Aug 21 still reads D07 Torso in Torso's color, July 26 still reads
D03 Hamstrings, under a cycle that has neither day.

## Notes

`frontend/public/snapshot.db` is regenerated in this PR deliberately. It's baked into
the image; left on the old schema, anonymous visitors would read a snapshot the new
frontend can't parse until the 4-hourly cron caught up.

On merge, the deploy applies both migrations and the current-day pointer lands on
`pecs-mobility` — the same workout that was already coming up next, so the cutover
doesn't change what tomorrow is.

Two eslint errors in `App.jsx` (`__BUILD_NUMBER__`, `isAdmin`) are pre-existing and
untouched.

Continuous backup for the shared Cosmos account is being handled separately in
infra-bootstrap; it's an account-level, one-way change that affects the other apps on
that account, so it doesn't belong here.
title: Expand the cycle to 16 days, and identify days by slug
